Samsung's top flagship is 32% off on Amazon, dropping below $950 with its 200MP camera and Privacy Display.

Samsung’s best phone is back at one of its lowest prices for Black Friday. The unlocked Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is down to $949.99 on Amazon, which is $450 off its $1,399.99 list price and just $15 above its all-time low.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra’s standout feature is its built-in Privacy Display. Switch it on and the screen narrows its viewing angle, so people next to you on a train or in a coffee shop can’t easily read your messages. You can also set it to kick in for notifications or specific apps.

The display itself is excellent, with a 6.9-inch QHD+ AMOLED panel, a 120Hz refresh rate, and up to 2,600 nits of peak brightness. Behind it sits the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy, so performance is about as good as Android gets right now.

Photography is another highlight. The 200MP main camera now has a brighter f/1.4 aperture for better low-light shots, and it’s joined by a 50MP ultra-wide plus 3x and 50MP 5x telephoto cameras for flexible zoom.

A 5,000mAh battery and Super Fast Charging 3.0 keep it going through busy days, and the built-in S Pen is still on hand for notes and quick edits.

At $949.99, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra puts Samsung’s best display, cameras, and S Pen in your pocket for well under $1,000.

items.title: iPhone 18 Production Delay Leaves Apple Little Time Before Launch
items.summary: Apple's upcoming iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e models are reportedly suffering from another production delay. In a new post on Weibo, the leaker known as "Fixed Focus Digital" claimed that neither model has entered mass production, with the start pushed back from late October to around New Year's Day in…
items.body: Apple's upcoming iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e models are reportedly suffering from another production delay. In a new post on Weibo, the leaker known as "Fixed Focus Digital" claimed that neither model has entered mass production, with the start pushed back from late October to around New Year's Day in 2027. In October, the same source pointed to late November as the production target for the standard ‌iPhone 18‌ and suggested Apple was preparing to build a large inventory. The latest claim cites a different earlier deadline, but January would be later than either of the previously reported targets. Fixed Focus Digital previously suggested that Apple will use some of the same manufacturing processes and components for the two phones. The leaker recently shared a diagram purporting to show identical batteries and 6.3-inch displays for both, although reports disagree about whether the iPhone 18e's screen will increase in size. Expected upgrades include an A20 chip in both models , while other rumors point to 9GB of RAM , up from 8GB, and Apple's C2 modem. Larger batteries have also been rumored, with a potential front-facing camera upgrade for the iPhone 18e. Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman recently identified February or March as the expected introduction window for both devices. If that schedule holds, a January production start would give Apple less time than usual to accumulate stock before launch. items.summary: Additionally, Gemini Live could get a brand-new text box to type your request.
items.body:

Gemini Live is testing a new Activity tab for all your agentic tasks

Additionally, Gemini Live could get a brand-new text box to type your request.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 8:18 AM ET

•

•

Marvin Velasco / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• The Google Gemini app is testing a new Activity option containing Scheduled and Tasks tabs.

• These two tabs should let users check on their existing one-time tasks or ones they’ve scheduled to run periodically.

• Google is also working on a new text box for the Gemini Live experience, with traces of this particular addition appearing a couple of months ago.

Google Gemini already lets you create one-time or scheduled tasks using Gemini Live, and the app could soon let you access them more easily. We have spotted development on a new option that brings these two elements together.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

We looked into version 17.78.14 of the Google app to activate a new Activity option at the top of the Gemini Live interface, featuring tabs named Tasks and Scheduled. While we could surface both pages in our testing, neither displayed any of the tasks and scheduled actions we created.

The onscreen text leaves no ambiguity about what each tab is for, with Tasks displaying actions that you’ve assigned to run in the background, while the Scheduled tab is for tasks that you have scheduled to run periodically, like a daily news brief, for instance.

There’s also a close (X) button at the top left of the screen to return to the standard Gemini Live experience. It’s definitely a work in progress right now, so it’s hard to say whether these new options will roll out at some point.

Beyond these changes, the same version of the Google app also reveals a text box in Gemini Live. Right now, a blue pill-shaped button sits between the Gemini Live controls and functions as a visualizer. In an upcoming redesign, Google could remove this entirely and add a new text box where you can type your request.

This could be related to a feature we spotted in September, where Gemini Live would let users swipe up to access the keyboard. Adding a prominent text box there could save users the trouble of swiping up and jump straight into typing.

With this redesign, shortcuts for the plus menu, video, microphone, and close/exit may sit inside the text box, similar to the standard text-based Gemini experience.

The fact that we’ve seen traces of this feature in development in the past indicates it could see the light of day soon. Still, it would be unwise to say anything definitively right now, given that we had to manually activate the text field in the Gemini Live interface.

items.summary: The Health Coach can do something the manual workout builder can't.
items.body:

Wearables and health

Google Health won’t let users manually add rests between workout sets

The Health Coach can do something the manual workout builder can't.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 8:13 AM ET

•

•

Joe Maring / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Google Health’s manual workout builder lacks the option to schedule rests between sets, even though the Premium-exclusive Health Coach supports it.

• Live workout metrics can also fail to appear in the app, even with an active smartwatch connection.

• We’ve reached out to Google to find out whether fixes are in the works and when users can expect them.

One of the biggest fitness upgrades in the November Pixel Drop lets Pixel Watch 3, 4, and 5 owners follow workouts directly on their wrists, with timers and audio cues that tell them when to move on to the next set or exercise. But as more users get access to step-by-step workouts, a scheduling limitation for rest between sets and a bug affecting live workout metrics are taking some of the shine off the experience.

Multiple Google Health users on Reddit (1, 2, 3) report that while they can schedule rest periods between different exercises when building a custom workout, they can’t do the same between sets of an individual exercise.

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Google is also investigating a separate issue reported by a Pixel Watch 3 owner, where the live metrics bar in Google Health fails to display heart rate, cardio load, and calories burned during custom workouts despite the watch being connected.

items.title: Samsung is building a Siri-style Vision mode for its Camera app, along with Auto portrait
items.summary: Both features are likely bound for the Galaxy S27 series.
items.body:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Mobile

Samsung is building a Siri-style Vision mode for its Camera app, along with Auto portrait

Both features are likely bound for the Galaxy S27 series.

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 7:53 AM ET

•

•

Zac Kew-Denniss / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

TL;DR

• Code in One UI 9.5 Beta 1 points to a new “Vision mode” in Samsung’s Camera app. It will seemingly describe what you point at and hand off follow-up questions to Gemini.

• The same build also points to a new “Auto portrait” feature, which could add background blur in Photo mode whenever it spots a face or a pet.

• Neither feature works on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the code suggests both need new hardware, so they will likely debut on the Galaxy S27 series.

Pointing your camera at something and asking your phone about it isn’t really a new feature these days. Samsung shipped Bixby Vision with the Galaxy S8 back in 2017. Google has Lens and Circle to Search, and Gemini Live’s camera sharing has been on Android phones since last year. Apple was late to the party with Visual Intelligence. Then, with iOS 27, Apple moved Visual Intelligence to the Camera app, where a new Siri mode lives alongside Photo, Video, and other camera modes. Despite beating Apple to the punch, Samsung appears to be preparing its own refreshed version of this feature, seemingly borrowing from Apple’s UX. We dug through the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s One UI 9.5 Beta 1 firmware and found a new Vision mode in the Camera app, plus an Auto portrait feature for Photo mode.

However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

Vision mode could turn the Samsung Camera app into a point-and-ask tool

The Samsung Camera app has code for a new mode simply called Vision, which sits among the regular camera modes. When the feature launches, you could switch to it like any other mode in the Camera app.

Code

<string name="SM_VISION_AI">Vision</string>
<string name="vision_ai_generated_by_ai">This content was generated by AI</string>

When users switch to it, the shutter icon could animate into a new design, and the camera could start streaming the live preview to a new Samsung app called Visual Agent Service. Based on the code, it seems the mode will show a scene card with an AI-written summary of what’s in front of you, along with a row of tappable keywords, and a footer noting that the content was generated by AI. Below the card, Vision mode appears to show suggested actions (“nudges”), a text extraction button, and a flashlight toggle.

Vision mode will likely also have two buttons next to the shutter: Ask and Translate. If that layout sounds familiar, it’s because Apple’s Siri mode uses a similar setup: a description card at the top of the viewfinder and two buttons flanking the shutter.

Tapping Ask, or one of the keywords, appears to send the camera frame to the Gemini app, along with the keyword’s question if you tapped one. Code shows that this will also copy that question to your clipboard. Translate will likely hand the camera viewfinder frame to Samsung’s AI Vision app instead (a separate app from the Camera app’s Vision mode).

Notably, pressing the shutter in Vision mode doesn’t appear to save a photo. It will likely only freeze the viewfinder preview, so you can ask questions about it.

You can already do much of this on your Galaxy phone today: simply open Gemini Live and share your camera.

Rita El Khoury / Android Authority

What would set Vision mode apart, if Samsung ships it as the code describes, is that it would be built into the Camera app and would give you Samsung’s own scene summary before you reach Gemini. We couldn’t tell whether that summary is generated on your phone or in the cloud, as that work happens inside Visual Agent Service, which currently isn’t available on the S26 Ultra.

Vision mode leans on what’s left of Bixby Vision for translation

The AI Vision app looks to be what’s left of Bixby Vision. It keeps the same package name, and some of its strings still say “Welcome to Bixby Vision.”

On the S26 Ultra, the AI Vision app no longer has an app drawer icon. Instead, it opens only from the camera, where it appears to power the Real-time translation feature that debuted with the Galaxy S26 series. The old Bixby Vision button in the camera’s More menu was already hidden in One UI 9, so Vision mode in the Camera app isn’t replacing it so much as bringing point-and-ask back to the camera in a new form.

When we pointed the camera at Hindi text on the S26 Ultra, the AI Vision app overlaid an English translation within a few seconds. Samsung’s own translation engine handled it on the phone, though this could change on newer phones, as the AI Vision app has picked up a new setting in One UI 9.5 for processing data on-device:

Code

<string name="setting_process_data_only_on_device">Process data only on device</string>
<string name="setting_process_data_only_on_device_summary">For added privacy, process AI Vision data on your device instead of online.</string>
<string name="cloud_translation_on_device_only_guide">To translate without signing in to your Samsung account, turn on Process data only on device in Settings.</string>

The app also has new strings for network errors, a consent screen for translation, and a content filter. There’s even a fallback message saying it will use on-device translation if the phone can’t connect. Together, they point to cloud translation for users signed in to a Samsung account.

Code

<string name="live_trans_network_unavailable_use_on_device_toast">Couldn't connect to the network. On-device translation will be used instead.</string>
<string name="live_trans_network_unavailable_try_again_toast">Couldn't connect to the network. Check your connection and try again.</string>
<string name="translation_onboarding_consent_body">To continue, agree to the %1$sTerms and Conditions%2$s, the %3$sPrivacy Notice%4$s, and then agree to the additional required agreements. The Privacy Notice lets you know how we handle your personal information.</string>
<string name="safety_filter_error">Can't translate text because it might contain inappropriate content.</string>
<string name="text_translator_safety_filter_error">This content can't be translated.</string>
<string name="safety_filter_sa_token_error">Check Samsung account error.</string>

The on-device setting appears only on phones with a newer Galaxy AI version than the S26 Ultra’s, outside China, and it appears to be off by default. On older phones like the S26 Ultra, the app always translates on the phone, which is why the setting doesn’t show up.

Camera app’s Auto portrait could add blur without switching to Portrait mode

The Samsung Camera app has another new feature in the works, called Portrait effect in Photo, which the code refers to as Auto portrait. It appears to apply background blur automatically in Photo mode when it detects a face or a pet. You could also turn it on manually from the viewfinder, with a slider to adjust blur strength.

Code

<string name="Title_Portrait_effect_in_photo">Portrait effect in Photo</string>
<string name="bokeh_effect_blur">Blur</string>

If this sounds familiar, Apple added something similar with the iPhone 15. When newer iPhones detect a person, cat, or dog in the shot, the camera automatically captures depth data without using Portrait mode, so you can turn the photo into a portrait later in the Photos app.

Based on the code, Samsung’s take appears to work differently: when the effect kicks in, the camera appears to switch to a dedicated Auto portrait capture mode, so the blur is applied as you shoot rather than saved for later.

Neither Vision mode nor Auto portrait currently works on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the code suggests both need hardware the phone doesn’t have, making the Galaxy S27 series the obvious candidate. The S27 series is rumored to launch in January, so we may not have long to wait to see whether Samsung’s Vision mode can stand next to Apple’s Siri mode within their respective camera apps.

Samsung has not officially announced either feature. We’ll keep you updated when we learn more.

The on-device setting appears only on phones with a newer Galaxy AI version than the S26 Ultra’s, outside China, and it appears to be off by default. On older phones like the S26 Ultra, the app always translates on the phone, which is why the setting doesn’t show up.
Camera app’s Auto portrait could add blur without switching to Portrait mode

The Samsung Camera app has another new feature in the works, called Portrait effect in Photo, which the code refers to as Auto portrait. It appears to apply background blur automatically in Photo mode when it detects a face or a pet. You could also turn it on manually from the viewfinder, with a slider to adjust blur strength.

If this sounds familiar, Apple added something similar with the iPhone 15. When newer iPhones detect a person, cat, or dog in the shot, the camera automatically captures depth data without using Portrait mode, so you can turn the photo into a portrait later in the Photos app.

Based on the code, Samsung’s take appears to work differently: when the effect kicks in, the camera appears to switch to a dedicated Auto portrait capture mode, so the blur is applied as you shoot rather than saved for later.

Neither Vision mode nor Auto portrait currently works on the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the code suggests both need hardware the phone doesn’t have, making the Galaxy S27 series the obvious candidate. The S27 series is rumored to launch in January, so we may not have long to wait to see whether Samsung’s Vision mode can stand next to Apple’s Siri mode within their respective camera apps.
Samsung has not officially announced either feature. We’ll keep you updated when we learn more.

It could also peek at your screen to answer your questions better.

TL;DR

• OpenAI is testing more features for the ChatGPT app on Android to let it control parts of your phone.

• Based on the evidence we found, ChatGPT could make calls, send or receive SMSes, control media playback, and even view what’s on your screen.

• OpenAI is also testing broader utility for Dots to accomplish more on Android.

If you’re fond of ChatGPT and prefer it over Gemini, you can already assign it as the default assistant on your Android devices. Even then, its current abilities remain limited to Voice mode and responding to your queries in text only. But now, OpenAI could be working on giving ChatGPT more control on your Android device — with your permission.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

OpenAI appears to be working on deeper ChatGPT integration in Android, where the assistant could soon do more than just chat with you. We’ve dug up references to ChatGPT’s upcoming abilities to make calls, send text messages, control media, and so much more.

ChatGPT could make calls and reply to messages

In version 1.2026.328, we found strings associated with permissions that ChatGPT could request before looking through your call history, placing calls for you, looking up your contacts, or reading and sending text messages.

Code

I need access to your phone’s contacts to finish this lookup.

Let ChatGPT read recent calls on this phone, including phone numbers and saved names.

Allow this workspace to place calls from your phone?

Allow this workspace to read and send text messages on your phone?

Let ChatGPT place phone calls from this phone when you ask.

It could control media playback

Along with these, certain other strings hint at the possibility of letting ChatGPT find and control media on your phone using notifications access. ChatGPT could play, pause, or skip tracks on Android devices, as per the following strings.

Code

Let ChatGPT find and control media playing on this phone

Allow this workspace to find and control media playing on your phone?

Allow notification access for ChatGPT in Android Settings, then return to this request to continue.

Pause, resume, or skip tracks on this phone. ChatGPT uses Android notification access to control playback.

Another permissions-related string reveals ChatGPT might be able to look up local media players, determine their existing states, and the actions they allow. Along with that, ChatGPT could identify the artist and track, potentially to learn your preferences or recommend music. However, it may not be able to directly launch media players or play or resume a particular track if that information isn’t visible in notifications.

Code

Read the current local media players on this Android phone, their playback state, supported actions, and available title and artist.

Resume means play the existing session; this tool does not open an app or choose new music.

After a verified resume, finish without any spoken follow-up so you do not interrupt the music.

When used, ChatGPT could also verify whether the outcome matches what was desired. However, there may not be a verbal confirmation or follow-up since that might interrupt media playback.

Or read what’s on your screen

Besides controlling media playback and making calls or sending texts for you, ChatGPT might be able to view what’s on your screen and use it as context to help you with queries.

Code

Read what is currently visible on this Android phone's screen. Call this tool again for every new question about the current screen, including follow-ups

Ask about your screen

Turn on “Use screen and app data”

The strings related to this feature suggest ChatGPT could pull up a new screenshot in response to every follow-up question about what’s on your screen.

And connect to Dots

Certain other permissions we spotted cite a Dot card, likely referring to ChatGPT’s eponymous always-on agent that executes tasks without requiring you to keep the app active.

Code

Use the same Dot card. After granting notification access in Android Settings, return to that card and tap Connect if prompted, or Continue.

With reference to Dots, we also see two configurations in the code:

Code

allowedWhileLocked

useDotAsAssistant

The former of the two suggests ChatGPT might be able to hail Dots even when the phone is locked, while the latter hints at the possibility of allowing users to use a particular Dot as the digital assistant on their phone.

The extent to which Dots might have access to Android devices remains unclear. Beyond these strings — and speculations based on the text, we don’t have evidence showing exactly how these features could function. We’re unsure when we might be able to see it in action, but we’ll share updates whenever it happens.

items.summary: U.S. smartphone shipments fell 9% year-over-year in the third quarter of 2026, and yet Apple grew its share of the market from 50% to 57%, according to the latest U.S. Market Monitor data from Counterpoint Research . Apple was the only major manufacturer to avoid a shipment decline in the quarter. C…
items.body: U.S. smartphone shipments fell 9% year-over-year in the third quarter of 2026, and yet Apple grew its share of the market from 50% to 57%, according to the latest U.S. Market Monitor data from Counterpoint Research . Apple was the only major manufacturer to avoid a shipment decline in the quarter. Counterpoint put the wider market decline down to rising memory costs, which hit Android manufacturers hardest at the low end. Thin margins leave little room for these vendors to absorb higher component prices without raising their prices or cutting volume. Samsung held its ground at 25% share, up one point year-over-year, thanks to its flagship Galaxy S and Z series devices and the low-end Galaxy A-series. But it was Motorola that took the biggest hit – its share fell four points to 8% as memory costs squeezed its large low-end lineup, essentially reversing the share growth it posted in the second quarter. Meanwhile, Google's Pixel 11 launch was not strong enough to prevent a slight decline in share. Smartphone sales at the Big Three carriers already declined 4% year-over-year in Q3, and Counterpoint similarly expects weak Q4 sales as consumers increasingly time purchases around the best deals. Last month, Counterpoint's global third-quarter data likewise showed Apple gaining share in a shrinking smartphone market . TL;DR

• Google is working on a new “Today” feed for Collections in the Play Store.

• It combines recommendations from multiple apps into a single feed.

• Users can also choose which apps contribute content to the feed.

It’s been a while since Google first introduced Collections in the Play Store, and the feature has largely remained unchanged, barring some new widgets we spotted the company working on. Although Collections is quite good at organizing content from your installed apps into separate categories, Google is now working on a new feed that brings all of these recommendations together.

APK teardown

This reporting is based on work-in-progress code. These features may not ship.

You're reading an Android Authority exclusive story you won’t find anywhere else. An APK teardown helps predict features that may arrive on a service in the future based on work-in-progress code. However, it is possible that such predicted features may not make it to a public release. More Authority Insights →

While digging through the latest version of the Google Play Store (v54.4.11), we found evidence of Google working on a new “Today” feed inside Collections. With a bit of tinkering, we managed to enable it on our device. The new tab appears right next to “App Library,” ahead of the existing content categories.

We also spotted a new pop-up that could show up the first time a user opens Collections after the feature rolls out. In the Today feed, you will be able to browse recommendations from multiple apps in one place instead of switching between individual collections. On our test device, the feed showed favorite playlists from Spotify alongside game recommendations from the Play Store.

Google is also adding customization options for the new Today feed. Just like with other feeds in Collections, you can choose which apps contribute content to the Today feed. The list includes apps like Google Maps, Play Books, Play Store, Spotify, YouTube, and YouTube Music, along with any other app that’s supported in the different collection categories. You can also change the position of the Today tab or remove it from Collections entirely.

The new Today collection isn’t live yet, and we only managed to turn it on with a bit of tinkering. However, it seems to be working as expected. Hopefully, Google will roll it out soon.

Gemini ran my errands on the Pixel 10 like I was in a sci-fi movie

Want to spend your time watching Gemini use your phone?

•

Nov 27, 2026 — 6:30 AM ET

•

•

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

Add Android Authority on Google:

Preferred Source

Google Discover

Gemini Intelligence isn’t just a marketing term that Google slaps onto its Pixel phones. It enables a bunch of handy AI features, including task automation — the dream use case for artificial intelligence. A whole bouquet of these automations recently made their way to last year’s Pixel 10 in newer regions, after debuting on the Pixel 11, and I couldn’t keep myself from giving it a go.

Gemini can already work inside a few apps in the backend, but it can now interact with third-party apps just like you do, using the same visual interface. It brings to reality the idea of AI taking over your mundane tasks like a true assistant. After living with Gemini Intelligence on the Pixel 10, I feel like I’ve had a taste of the future.

Readers' poll

Would you use Gemini's task automation instead of navigating apps yourself?

2 votes

Setting up Gemini’s task automations on the Pixel 10

Google

As confusing as it may be, Gemini can interact with other apps in two ways. One is through connectors that let it work in the app in the background without needing to interact with the user-facing interface, but this new automation feature that we are talking about today allows Gemini to work with the same UI that you and I see, with the help of taps and scrolls, to get the job done, opening up Gemini to more third-party apps that don’t yet have a Gemini connector.

While the Pixel 11 series has had the feature since launch, the latest November QPR update introduced the feature to the Pixel 10 series in certain regions (India, Japan, and the UK, in addition to the US). A handful of recent Samsung flagships are also supported, so you need to have one of the compatible devices with the latest update installed to use Gemini’s on-screen automations. Having said that, there was no Gemini setting to flick it on in my case (Google’s official docs say there is), leaving you at Google’s mercy and its erratic server-side rollout, even if you have the latest update installed.

To check whether the feature is available to you, you have to directly ask Gemini to do something in one of the supported apps — we recently uncovered a hidden list of apps that Gemini supports for task automations, and that is also the only way to enable it. To give Gemini permission to work inside apps, a small pop-up will appear after you give your command, where you can allow Gemini to proceed. You’ll have to do this for each app you want Gemini to use for you.

First-party vs. third-party app automations

Akshay Gangwar / Android Authority

As you’d expect, Google’s own services worked absolutely perfectly. It almost feels like the ideal future where you just delegate tasks, and they are handled for you without much back-and-forth. I’ve long used Google’s Spark, now called Gemini Tasks, to handle everyday Gmail responses, drafts, and changes inside Google Sheets without knowing every single one of those thousands of formulas. I frequently use it to watch for emails I’m expecting or chase stubborn customer support reps.

Since Workspace apps and other Google products (Photos, YouTube, et al.) are directly connected to Gemini on the backend using Connectors, the AI doesn’t need to use the consumer-facing interface to get the task done. A handful of third-party apps can also work in a similar fashion, including popular names like Spotify, Wispr Flow, Granola, Canva, and Adobe. However, on-screen automations open up a lot more third-party apps, and they are surprisingly less frustrating to use than those with connectors.

Once Gemini starts finding its way around the app, you can see it in action in a small window. While app automations are intended to offload your errands onto the AI while you focus on more important things, the novelty is so fascinating that I couldn’t help but gape at it in astonishment, as if watching an infant take its first steps.

I couldn't help but gape at it in astonishment, as if watching an infant take its first steps.

I started with Uber and asked it to find me a few options for the airport and tell me if the prices were unusually high. It followed the same flow that I manually would have: checked the available options and got back to me with all the details, including trip costs across vehicle options, which it confirmed didn’t include any surge prices. The results were similarly satisfactory when I asked it to add a few grocery items and repeat my coffee order from a few weeks ago on Blinkit and Zomato (equivalent to Instacart and DoorDash, respectively), though it required a bit of back-and-forth.

Do note that Gemini won’t make the final payment and will come back to you when it’s done with its part and ask you to review the final checkout page and make the payment. So, you don’t have to worry about AI wiping out your account (just yet). And on the preview page, you can either stop the automated task at any point or take over the screen if you think Gemini is running astray.

What worked and what didn’t

I started this test with a bit of skepticism because my experience with third-party connectors hasn’t been completely perfect. I’ve had to take back control because Gemini either didn’t understand what I wanted or required so much effort that it was easier to do it manually. Thankfully, on-screen automation has proven to be far more reliable in my testing — enough that I can delegate the task without actively reviewing it in real time, so I can shift my focus to other, more pressing things.

If I were to put a number to it, I would rate it 8 out of 10 because there were a few moments where it needed my intervention. The Uber experiment went quite well, except once when the phone froze during previewing, so we’ll put that aside, but while cross-checking an old order, it repeated the entire order instead of just the coffee I had asked it to. On another occasion, when I wanted to see if Zomato (a food ordering service) allowed scheduling, it had trouble scrolling up the wheel picker because its scroll gestures on the screen were far too long, something that we as humans intuitively know.

My biggest annoyance with the whole experience wasn't the automation feature itself, but the lack of continued conversation in Gemini for Android.

On another occasion, when filling up my cart with groceries, Gemini failed to add the right product or added replacements that I wouldn’t pick, which required me to ask it to search my order history and pick only the products that I frequently order, which again worked pretty well. More interestingly, if I couldn’t remember the specific name of a product, I could simply describe the packaging — like, “add the blue-colored milk carton that I frequently order” — and it would follow.

As you can tell, none of these are deal breakers but minor inconveniences that could easily be solved with a future update. In fact, I’m rather impressed by how nearly flawlessly everything works. Having said that, my biggest annoyance with the whole experience wasn’t the automation feature itself, but the lack of continued conversation in Gemini for Android. Each time Gemini returned the result, I had to switch on the mic to talk to it. Before you point it out, on-screen automations don’t work inside Gemini Live, at least they didn’t for me.

Did Gemini actually make my day easier?

Megan Ellis / Android Authority

I wish I was using the time when Gemini was working on the errand to do something else, but I was busy marveling at my phone automatically, almost magically, doing things. But I hope, as the novelty wears off, like it has with other AI tools I use to manage work on my desktop, it will prove to be a solid helping hand to take over the routine tasks that don’t require too much attention. Of course, I can still take over manually when, say, I’m ordering something different or special instead of repeating my past orders.

And with routine use of on-screen automation, I now understand the gaps that often require Gemini to follow up with me, like when something is out of stock or it adds extra dishes to my cart. I can add those restrictions or workarounds in my first prompt itself to minimize my manual interventions. And I’m sure, as Gemini learns more about my preferences, it will get even better at predicting them by itself, requiring me only at the checkout page for final confirmation and payment.

But even today in its current form, Gemini’s on-screen task automation has brought us closer to the Jarvis-like sci-fi reality, and I’m all for it.

The Roborock Saros 20 Flow ($1699.99 at Amazon) is one of the company’s most expensive robot vacuum cleaners, bringing major upgrades to mopping and hands-free maintenance, along with 36,000Pa suction. It’s also one of the most feature-packed robot vacuums I’ve tested in a while, with plenty that makes everyday cleaning a lot easier. But does it do enough to justify its hefty price tag and earn a spot among the best robot vacuums you can buy? Let’s find out.

There’s a lot going on with the Roborock Saros 20 Flow

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Roborock seems to have taken some inspiration from Qualcomm when it comes to naming its products (that’s how confusing the lineup is right now). There’s the Qrevo series of robot vacuums, the F25 series of cordless wet-dry vacuums, and then there’s the company’s flagship Saros 20 lineup, which currently includes three models: the Saros 20, the Saros 20 Flow, and the Saros 20 Sonic.

While all three are premium robot vacuums, the biggest difference is how they handle mopping. The regular Saros 20 uses traditional rotating mop pads, while the Saros 20 Sonic, which costs the same $1,699.99 as the Flow, uses a vibrating mop pad. The Saros 20 Flow, on the other hand, comes with a roller mop that’s designed to clean itself continuously as it moves across your floors.

In terms of design, the Saros 20 Flow looks much like any other premium robot vacuum. It has a circular body with two side brushes at the front, a roller mop at the back, and a retractable LiDAR sensor on top. Interestingly, despite having a retractable LiDAR sensor, the Saros 20 Flow is slightly taller than the regular Saros 20, measuring 3.54 inches compared to 3.14 inches. This means it might struggle to get underneath certain pieces of furniture that the regular model can reach, although I didn’t run into many issues with this during my testing.

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

The docking station is also quite large, but that’s because it handles most of the maintenance for you. There are two separate water tanks for clean and dirty water, a compartment for cleaning solution, and a dust bag that collects everything the vacuum picks up.

Thankfully, Roborock has made the initial setup straightforward. Most of the components come pre-installed, so all you really need to do is attach the base tray, plug in the power cord, and you’re good to go. Pairing the vacuum with your phone is just as easy. You simply scan the QR code on the unit, and the Roborock app takes care of the rest.

The roller mop is the real star of the show

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Coming back to the robot vacuum itself, one of the biggest highlights of the Saros 20 Flow is its roller mop. Unlike traditional robot vacuums that use rotating mop pads, the Saros 20 Flow uses a continuously rotating roller that gets cleaned with fresh water as it mops. This means the vacuum isn’t simply dragging the same dirty mop across your floors, which is particularly useful if you have a lot of hard flooring in your home.

The suction power is equally impressive, with the same 36,000Pa suction we saw on the Saros 20. It also features Roborock’s AdaptiLift Traverse 3.0 system, which allows the vacuum to raise its chassis and cross two-step thresholds up to a combined height of 8.8cm (3.46 inches), with the first step up to 4.5cm (1.77 inches). This helps if you have raised door thresholds or uneven flooring between rooms.

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

As for the actual cleaning experience, one thing that immediately stood out to me was just how quiet the Saros 20 Flow is. Despite having such powerful suction, it’s noticeably quieter than several other robot vacuums I’ve tested. Of course, it gets louder when you crank up the suction, but for everyday cleaning, I didn’t find the noise particularly bothersome.

I also like how little I had to intervene once everything was set up. The Roborock app uses AI to automatically determine the suction power, water usage, and cleaning sequence based on the room and how dirty the floor is. You can manually adjust all these settings whenever you want, but I found the automatic mode worked well for most cleaning sessions.

In terms of features, there is AI dirt detection onboard as well. This means the robot vacuum can automatically recognize dirty spots on the floor and go over them again if needed, without you having to tell it to do so.

Cleaning performance is excellent, with a few caveats

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

If there’s one thing I didn’t particularly like about the Saros 20 Flow’s cleaning performance, it’s the edge cleaning. The Saros 20 Flow has an extendable roller mop that moves out from the side of the robot vacuum to clean along walls and edges. However, I found the results to be a bit hit or miss.

There were several instances where the vacuum left certain spots unmopped or uncleaned, even when cleaning along a perfectly straight wall. It’s not a dealbreaker by any means, but it’s something I noticed more than once during my testing. That said, this is my biggest complaint after using the Saros 20 Flow for the past few weeks. If mopping is your priority and you have a lot of hard flooring in your home, the Saros 20 Flow is hard to beat.

As for battery life, I found it to be pretty good, especially considering the size of my home. I tested the Saros 20 Flow in a roughly 2,500-square-foot home with three bedrooms, a large living area, and plenty of furniture. During a full cleaning session, with vacuuming followed by mopping, the battery dropped to around 35% by the time it finished. That’s impressive considering how much ground it had to cover, and if you’re using it for occasional cleaning or have a smaller home, battery life shouldn’t be much of a concern.

The Roborock Saros 20 Flow cleaned my roughly 2,500-square-foot home with around 35% battery to spare.

The water tanks, however, are a different story. During the same cleaning session, I had to refill the clean water tank and empty the dirty water tank midway through. This will depend on how large your home is and how dirty the floors are, but it’s worth keeping in mind if you’re planning to use the vacuum in a similarly large space.

In terms of cleaning speed, the Saros 20 Flow took around three hours to completely clean my home. It’s worth noting that I used a cleaning cycle where the vacuum first cleaned the floors and then went over them again with the mop, rather than the default setting, which does both simultaneously. The overall cleaning time should be considerably shorter if you choose to vacuum and mop together.

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Another area where the Saros 20 Flow impressed me was obstacle avoidance. It can recognize different household objects and navigate around them without getting stuck. During my testing, it successfully identified shoes and loose cables on the floor and avoided them without any intervention. And yes, this also means that the Saros 20 Flow has a built-in camera that helps identify objects, and you can even enable an option in the Roborock app to capture photos of what it avoids.

There’s also a remote monitoring feature that lets you use the robot’s camera to check on your home. However, I didn’t end up using this feature because I don’t particularly want another surveillance camera inside my house.

Apart from occasionally dealing with the water tanks, the Saros 20 Flow pretty much takes care of itself.

Once the cleaning is done, the Saros 20 Flow automatically returns to its docking station and starts cleaning the roller mop. By default, the mop washing cycle is set to Balanced, but you can also choose a more intensive cleaning mode that uses water heated to as much as 100°C (212°F). This helps remove dirt and grime from the roller without you having to wash it manually.

After washing, the docking station also dries the mop using warm air over the next few hours. This helps prevent moisture buildup and unpleasant odors, while ensuring the mop is clean and ready for the next session. It’s one of the things I really appreciate about the Saros 20 Flow, because apart from occasionally refilling the clean water tank and emptying the dirty one, there’s very little maintenance you actually need to worry about.

Roborock Saros 20 Flow review verdict: Should you buy it?

Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

There’s no doubt that the Roborock Saros 20 Flow is an excellent cleaning machine. If you’re looking for a one-stop cleaning solution for your home and don’t want to compromise on features, the Saros 20 Flow is easily one of the best options you can buy right now.

Sure, this is an extremely expensive robot vacuum, and you can easily find a capable model for less than half its price. But if you have the budget and want something that takes care of almost everything on its own, the Saros 20 Flow is definitely worth considering.

What I particularly love about the Saros 20 Flow is how well it handles mopping. For someone like me who has a lot of hard flooring at home, the continuously cleaned roller mop makes a pretty big difference. Add to that the powerful 36,000Pa suction, automatic mop washing and drying, and the feature-rich Roborock app, and there’s very little left to complain about. I do wish the edge cleaning were a little more consistent, and the water tanks lasted longer, but those are my only real complaints after spending the past few weeks with it.

For someone like me who has a lot of hard flooring at home, the Saros 20 Flow's continuously cleaned roller mop makes a pretty big difference.

That said, there’s plenty of competition at this price point. There’s the Narwal Flow 2 ($949.99 at Narwal) and the Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone, both of which offer roller mops and automatic maintenance docks. There’s also the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete ($1699.99 at Amazon), which offers 35,000Pa suction, dual rotating mop pads, automatic mop cleaning with hot water, and a slimmer design that should make it easier to clean underneath furniture.

If you want something slightly more affordable but still want a premium cleaning experience, there’s also Roborock’s own Saros 20 ($1599.99 at Amazon). It offers many of the same high-end features, including powerful suction, advanced obstacle avoidance, and automatic maintenance, but uses traditional rotating mop pads instead of the Saros 20 Flow’s roller mop. In fact, my colleague Jonathan found the Saros 20 to be the best robot vacuum he’s tested for edge cleaning, so it might actually be a better option if that’s a priority for you.

However, if you’re specifically looking for a robot vacuum with a roller mop, you don’t necessarily need to spend nearly $1,700 to get one. Roborock’s own Qrevo Curv 2 Flow $999.99 at Amazon offers a similar approach to mopping. It is considerably taller than the Saros 20 Flow, though, so it might not be able to get underneath some of the lower pieces of furniture in your home.

Powerful cleaning and excellent mopping at a premium price.

The Roborock Saros 20 Flow is a premium robot vacuum and mop with 36,000Pa suction, a continuously self-cleaning SpiraFlow 2.0 roller mop, and AI-powered obstacle recognition, alongside an ultra-slim 8.98cm design, 8.8cm threshold climbing, and an automated RockDock with hot-water mop washing and drying.

It’s also one of the most feature-packed robot vacuums I’ve tested in a while, with plenty that makes everyday cleaning a lot easier. But does it do enough to justify its hefty price tag and earn a spot among the best robot vacuums you can buy? Let’s find out.
There’s a lot going on with the Roborock Saros 20 Flow

blocks.alt: Roborock Saros 20 Flow robot vacuum resting on its docking station

blocks.text: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Roborock seems to have taken some inspiration from Qualcomm when it comes to naming its products (that’s how confusing the lineup is right now). There’s the Qrevo series of robot vacuums, the F25 series of cordless wet-dry vacuums, and then there’s the company’s flagship Saros 20 lineup, which currently includes three models: the Saros 20, the Saros 20 Flow, and the Saros 20 Sonic.

While all three are premium robot vacuums, the biggest difference is how they handle mopping. The regular Saros 20 uses traditional rotating mop pads, while the Saros 20 Sonic, which costs the same $1,699.99 as the Flow, uses a vibrating mop pad. The Saros 20 Flow, on the other hand, comes with a roller mop that’s designed to clean itself continuously as it moves across your floors.

In terms of design, the Saros 20 Flow looks much like any other premium robot vacuum. It has a circular body with two side brushes at the front, a roller mop at the back, and a retractable LiDAR sensor on top. Interestingly, despite having a retractable LiDAR sensor, the Saros 20 Flow is slightly taller than the regular Saros 20, measuring 3.54 inches compared to 3.14 inches. This means it might struggle to get underneath certain pieces of furniture that the regular model can reach, although I didn’t run into many issues with this during my testing.

blocks.alt: Front view of Roborock Saros 20 Flow on marble flooring

blocks.text: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

The docking station is also quite large, but that’s because it handles most of the maintenance for you. There are two separate water tanks for clean and dirty water, a compartment for cleaning solution, and a dust bag that collects everything the vacuum picks up.

Thankfully, Roborock has made the initial setup straightforward. Most of the components come pre-installed, so all you really need to do is attach the base tray, plug in the power cord, and you’re good to go. Pairing the vacuum with your phone is just as easy. You simply scan the QR code on the unit, and the Roborock app takes care of the rest.
The roller mop is the real star of the show

blocks.alt: Underside of Roborock Saros 20 Flow showing roller mop and brushes

blocks.text: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Coming back to the robot vacuum itself, one of the biggest highlights of the Saros 20 Flow is its roller mop. Unlike traditional robot vacuums that use rotating mop pads, the Saros 20 Flow uses a continuously rotating roller that gets cleaned with fresh water as it mops. This means the vacuum isn’t simply dragging the same dirty mop across your floors, which is particularly useful if you have a lot of hard flooring in your home.

The suction power is equally impressive, with the same 36,000Pa suction we saw on the Saros 20. It also features Roborock’s AdaptiLift Traverse 3.0 system, which allows the vacuum to raise its chassis and cross two-step thresholds up to a combined height of 8.8cm (3.46 inches), with the first step up to 4.5cm (1.77 inches). This helps if you have raised door thresholds or uneven flooring between rooms.

blocks.alt: Roborock Saros 20 Flow showing its raised LiDAR navigation sensor

blocks.text: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

As for the actual cleaning experience, one thing that immediately stood out to me was just how quiet the Saros 20 Flow is. Despite having such powerful suction, it’s noticeably quieter than several other robot vacuums I’ve tested. Of course, it gets louder when you crank up the suction, but for everyday cleaning, I didn’t find the noise particularly bothersome.

I also like how little I had to intervene once everything was set up. The Roborock app uses AI to automatically determine the suction power, water usage, and cleaning sequence based on the room and how dirty the floor is. You can manually adjust all these settings whenever you want, but I found the automatic mode worked well for most cleaning sessions.

In terms of features, there is AI dirt detection onboard as well. This means the robot vacuum can automatically recognize dirty spots on the floor and go over them again if needed, without you having to tell it to do so.
Cleaning performance is excellent, with a few caveats

blocks.alt: Roborock Saros 20 Flow illuminating the floor beneath furniture

blocks.text: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

If there’s one thing I didn’t particularly like about the Saros 20 Flow’s cleaning performance, it’s the edge cleaning. The Saros 20 Flow has an extendable roller mop that moves out from the side of the robot vacuum to clean along walls and edges. However, I found the results to be a bit hit or miss.

There were several instances where the vacuum left certain spots unmopped or uncleaned, even when cleaning along a perfectly straight wall. It’s not a dealbreaker by any means, but it’s something I noticed more than once during my testing. That said, this is my biggest complaint after using the Saros 20 Flow for the past few weeks. If mopping is your priority and you have a lot of hard flooring in your home, the Saros 20 Flow is hard to beat.

As for battery life, I found it to be pretty good, especially considering the size of my home. I tested the Saros 20 Flow in a roughly 2,500-square-foot home with three bedrooms, a large living area, and plenty of furniture. During a full cleaning session, with vacuuming followed by mopping, the battery dropped to around 35% by the time it finished. That’s impressive considering how much ground it had to cover, and if you’re using it for occasional cleaning or have a smaller home, battery life shouldn’t be much of a concern.
The Roborock Saros 20 Flow cleaned my roughly 2,500-square-foot home with around 35% battery to spare.

The water tanks, however, are a different story. During the same cleaning session, I had to refill the clean water tank and empty the dirty water tank midway through. This will depend on how large your home is and how dirty the floors are, but it’s worth keeping in mind if you’re planning to use the vacuum in a similarly large space.

In terms of cleaning speed, the Saros 20 Flow took around three hours to completely clean my home. It’s worth noting that I used a cleaning cycle where the vacuum first cleaned the floors and then went over them again with the mop, rather than the default setting, which does both simultaneously. The overall cleaning time should be considerably shorter if you choose to vacuum and mop together.

blocks.alt: Roborock Saros 20 Flow docking station opened to reveal dust bag

blocks.text: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

Another area where the Saros 20 Flow impressed me was obstacle avoidance. It can recognize different household objects and navigate around them without getting stuck. During my testing, it successfully identified shoes and loose cables on the floor and avoided them without any intervention. And yes, this also means that the Saros 20 Flow has a built-in camera that helps identify objects, and you can even enable an option in the Roborock app to capture photos of what it avoids.

There’s also a remote monitoring feature that lets you use the robot’s camera to check on your home. However, I didn’t end up using this feature because I don’t particularly want another surveillance camera inside my house.
Apart from occasionally dealing with the water tanks, the Saros 20 Flow pretty much takes care of itself.

Once the cleaning is done, the Saros 20 Flow automatically returns to its docking station and starts cleaning the roller mop. By default, the mop washing cycle is set to Balanced, but you can also choose a more intensive cleaning mode that uses water heated to as much as 100°C (212°F). This helps remove dirt and grime from the roller without you having to wash it manually.

After washing, the docking station also dries the mop using warm air over the next few hours. This helps prevent moisture buildup and unpleasant odors, while ensuring the mop is clean and ready for the next session. It’s one of the things I really appreciate about the Saros 20 Flow, because apart from occasionally refilling the clean water tank and emptying the dirty one, there’s very little maintenance you actually need to worry about.
Roborock Saros 20 Flow review verdict: Should you buy it?

blocks.alt: Roborock Saros 20 Flow parked beneath its docking station

blocks.text: Sanuj Bhatia / Android Authority

There’s no doubt that the Roborock Saros 20 Flow is an excellent cleaning machine. If you’re looking for a one-stop cleaning solution for your home and don’t want to compromise on features, the Saros 20 Flow is easily one of the best options you can buy right now.

Sure, this is an extremely expensive robot vacuum, and you can easily find a capable model for less than half its price. But if you have the budget and want something that takes care of almost everything on its own, the Saros 20 Flow is definitely worth considering.

What I particularly love about the Saros 20 Flow is how well it handles mopping. For someone like me who has a lot of hard flooring at home, the continuously cleaned roller mop makes a pretty big difference. Add to that the powerful 36,000Pa suction, automatic mop washing and drying, and the feature-rich Roborock app, and there’s very little left to complain about. I do wish the edge cleaning were a little more consistent, and the water tanks lasted longer, but those are my only real complaints after spending the past few weeks with it.
For someone like me who has a lot of hard flooring at home, the Saros 20 Flow's continuously cleaned roller mop makes a pretty big difference.

That said, there’s plenty of competition at this price point. There’s the Narwal Flow 2 ($949.99 at Narwal) and the Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone, both of which offer roller mops and automatic maintenance docks. There’s also the Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete ($1699.99 at Amazon), which offers 35,000Pa suction, dual rotating mop pads, automatic mop cleaning with hot water, and a slimmer design that should make it easier to clean underneath furniture.

If you want something slightly more affordable but still want a premium cleaning experience, there’s also Roborock’s own Saros 20 ($1599.99 at Amazon). It offers many of the same high-end features, including powerful suction, advanced obstacle avoidance, and automatic maintenance, but uses traditional rotating mop pads instead of the Saros 20 Flow’s roller mop. In fact, my colleague Jonathan found the Saros 20 to be the best robot vacuum he’s tested for edge cleaning, so it might actually be a better option if that’s a priority for you.

However, if you’re specifically looking for a robot vacuum with a roller mop, you don’t necessarily need to spend nearly $1,700 to get one. Roborock’s own Qrevo Curv 2 Flow $999.99 at Amazon offers a similar approach to mopping. It is considerably taller than the Saros 20 Flow, though, so it might not be able to get underneath some of the lower pieces of furniture in your home.
Roborock Saros 20 Flow
Powerful cleaning and excellent mopping at a premium price.

The Roborock Saros 20 Flow is a premium robot vacuum and mop with 36,000Pa suction, a continuously self-cleaning SpiraFlow 2.0 roller mop, and AI-powered obstacle recognition, alongside an ultra-slim 8.98cm design, 8.8cm threshold climbing, and an automated RockDock with hot-water mop washing and drying.

items.body: Next year's iPhone 20 Pro models will make extensive use of 3D-printed titanium in their frames, based on the latest rumor coming out of China. In a new post on Weibo, the leaker known as "Fixed Focus Digital" claims that Apple plans to manufacture parts of the device's mid-frame using a laser-based titanium powder 3D-printing process – one which would result in significantly improved durability. The leaker is apparently so confident in the accuracy of the rumour that they even suggested followers take screenshots of the Weibo post and reference it next year when the device is announced. Earlier this month, Fixed Focus Digital claimed that Apple would return to titanium for next year's 20th-anniversary iPhone models. The iPhone 18 Pro models currently use aluminum frames. Apple already uses the 3D-printing technique to produce the titanium cases of the Apple Watch Ultra 4 and titanium Apple Watch Series 12 models, after the company debuted the process with the Ultra 3 and Series 11. Apple also uses it for the iPhone Air's USB-C port enclosure. The process involves using lasers to fuse successive layers of titanium powder. Apple says this allows for more complex structural designs than conventional manufacturing methods, and significantly reduces material waste. The technology could give Apple greater design flexibility as it develops its rumored all-glass 20th-anniversary iPhone design, which is expected to feature curved glass and virtually invisible display bezels . Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman has described the planned changes as the biggest overhaul of the Pro line since the iPhone X. What remains unclear is how Apple intends to address the thermal challenges associated with titanium, given the superior heat dissipation properties of the aluminum used in its current Pro models. Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 20 Pro series in the fall of 2027. Leakers have referred to the devices as the "iPhone 20 Pro," but Apple's actual naming plans are unknown. Tags: 20th-
